1:
The title detains three of them and irritates a fourth. Matthew Henry reports that some find Christ in the hind of the morning, marked out from eternity to be run down by the dogs that compass him, while others think it denotes only the tune. Adam Clarke canvasses the guesses — an instrument, a tune, a band of music, one editor rendering it a psalm addressed to the master who presided over the band called the Morning Hind — and then offers a better one: it may be the name of the psalm itself, since it was customary in the east to give poems names bearing no relation to their subject, and from manuscripts in his own collection he cites the Country of Roses, which says nothing of roses, the Gallery of Pictures, which contains no picture. John Calvin loses patience: the inscription is obscure, but interpreters have needlessly perplexed themselves seeking he knows not what sublime mystery in a matter of small importance, and the ancient expositors supposed that Christ would not be sufficiently honoured unless a mystical sense were forced upon the word.

Who speaks the opening cry is answered along the whole range. Keil and Delitzsch hold it David struggling upward out of the gloomiest depth during the persecution by Saul, and record the rival datings, one critic bringing the psalm down to the years before the destruction of the city and another to the exile, while a third closes his discussion by confessing that only one thing is certain. Charles Ellicott declines an individual altogether: the despairing tone suits the whole of pious Israel in her times of trouble even better than any single sufferer. Augustine of Hippo puts the words in the mouth of the crucified sustaining the person of the old man nailed to the cross with him, which is why the cry can speak of the words of my sins and be ignorant even of the reason for the forsaking. John Gill guards the same difficulty by distinctions: the personal union was not dissolved, nor did the sufferer cease to be loved, since the Father loved him because he laid down his life — what was lost was not the principle of joy but the act and the sense of it. John Wesley says the desertion was verified in part in David and much more fully in Christ. C.H. Spurgeon attends to the manner rather than the reference: faith beams forth in the doubled address, which keeps hold with both hands, and the divine name used signifies strength, so that the appeal is made in the agony of grief but not in the misery of doubt.

Charles Ellicott works over the wording. The word rendered roaring is used generally of a lion though also of a man; the closing clause of the next verse misses the parallelism, which requires that he cry in the night and find no repose; and he judges very plausible a conjecture that reads from my cry rather than from my help, since it completes the parallelism by a very slight change. On the throne of praises he is more expansive still: the phrase recalls the more usual dwelling between the cherubim but is more spiritual, the ever-ascending praises of his people becoming a throne for the divine King and taking the place of the outstretched wings. Adam Clarke keeps it to the sanctuary where praises are offered, and John Wesley to a people perpetually praising. John Gill makes the holiness a reason quieting the sufferer rather than an argument moving God, since one who bore the sins of others could justly be treated so. Adam Clarke ends the entry with a conjecture of place: the psalmist was at the spot where the father of the tribes had wrestled and been blessed, and may be heard asking whether he too, wrestling there, might not expect a similar success.
6:
Whether the sufferer can call himself a worm splits the entry at once. Adam Clarke says he can see no sense in which our Lord could use these terms, though David might well use them to express his vileness and worthlessness — and then quotes his old Psalter, which takes the words the other way entirely: I am a worm, that is, born of the maiden without man’s seed, and not man only but God also; and none the less I am the reproof of men, in spitting, in buffeting, in piercing with the thorns, and in being cast out by the people, who chose the thief and not me. John Wesley says the verse does not so truly agree to David as to Christ. Matthew Henry argues the same from the whole passage, since many of the particulars specified were never true of David and must therefore be appropriated to a greater sufferer in the depth of his humiliation. John Gill resolves it by shifting the ground of the name: it is used not of his origin, nor of his nature, but of the opinion men of the world had of him, one trodden underfoot as men tread worms. Charles Ellicott reads only extreme degradation and helplessness.

The mockery is examined word by word. Adam Clarke grants that the evangelist applies the shooting out of the lip to the conduct at the cross, but holds the words primarily true of the insults David suffered during the rebellion, the cases being so similar that the evangelist thought proper to describe the later conduct in the earlier language. Charles Ellicott notes that the old Greek here uses the very verb that appears in the gospel account of the crucifixion, and that the idiom for shooting out the lip is literally to open with the lip, where we say curl. He then raises a fork in the next clause: the old Greek, the evangelist and one modern read it as a report, he trusted on the Lord, but the form is generally taken as an imperative, so that the mockers say, roll thyself on God. John Gill expounds only the reported taunt, adding that the mockers jeered not at the object of his trust but at the trust itself, which they thought would be shown false. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the verb in the following verse, which can mean either to break forth from the womb or to push forward, and decline the reading that would make it the cause of his breaking forth.

The appeal to infancy draws out one polemic and one correction. John Gill uses it against those who claim something miraculous in the manner of the birth as well as in the conception: the conception was miraculous, being owing to the overshadowing of the Spirit, but the mother bore him the usual term of nine months as women commonly do, and he was brought forth as other infants are. Charles Ellicott corrects the connective to for, remarking that faith which turns to God in spite of derision is the best answer to derision, and would render the second clause not that God made him hope but that he made him repose on his mother’s breast. Adam Clarke keeps it simple, that God made him and guided him from earliest infancy. On the petition itself C.H. Spurgeon counts two reasons given and calls them a double knock at mercy’s gate, and dwells on the second: there is an awfulness about absolute friendlessness which is crushing to the human mind, since man was not made to be alone and is like a dismembered limb when he must endure heart-loneliness. Adam Clarke answers it in five words, that a present God is a present blessing, and John Gill distinguishes the presence withdrawn from the omnipresence that cannot be.
12:
The animals are read as classes of men. John Gill makes the bulls the chief priests and rulers together with the Gentile governors. Adam Clarke takes the bull as the emblem of brutal strength that gores and tramples, explains the district beyond Jordan as one where cattle were fattened until they grew the largest in the country. Keil and Delitzsch ground the epithet in the same pastures and add that a robustness acquired and used in opposition to God is brutish rather than human. Charles Ellicott locates the point of comparison elsewhere, in the wantonness and insolence of pampered pride displayed by the minions of fortune, and of the dogs he says they are literally barkers, which two ancient translators made hunting dogs, so that the enemies combine like savage animals to hunt in packs — for which he cites the wolves ravening in a black mist from Virgil. John Wesley keeps to insatiable greediness and implacable fierceness.

The dissolution of the sufferer’s body is where Adam Clarke breaks with the others. He gives the old Psalter’s version, that they reckoned no more of slaying him than of spilling water — and then says he cannot think there is any sound theologic sense in which these things can be spoken of Christ, either in the agony of the garden or in the death upon the cross. Keil and Delitzsch read the same verse in exactly the opposite way, taking the pouring out like water of the abandonment of the Crucified to a weakness in which life is dissolving, the parting of the bones of the forcible stretching out of the body, and the melting heart of the burning anguish, the inflammation of the wounds and the pressure of blood on head and heart, which they call the characteristic cause of that death. John Gill refers the same clause to the sweat in the garden or to the tears or to the blood. Charles Ellicott prefers that the bones stand out as in emaciation rather than being out of joint, and notes a conjecture at the next verse that reads my palate for my strength because it improves the parallelism, and sets the dust of death beside the way to dusty death in Shakespeare.

The hardest word in the psalm is treated at length by two of them. Adam Clarke lays out the apparatus: the received text as pointed reads as a lion, while the marginal reading gives they pierced; the Chaldee has biting as a lion my hands and my feet, but the Syriac, Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic and Arabic all read they pierced or digged; one great polyglot has the piercing in its text, others the lion, and the whole difference lies between two letters easily mistaken for one another. He decides for the piercing, and since the psalmist’s own hands were never pierced he lets the verse pass for a direct revelation. Charles Ellicott calls the word a battle-ground for controversy and agrees that no intelligible meaning can be got from as a lion, and that redividing the verses does not help, so that the pointing must be given up and the reading changed on the authority of the ancient versions, some manuscripts and the Masora. But he doubts the sense pierce altogether, and renders instead a band of villains surrounding him and binding his hands and feet so as to cut them. John Wesley says only that the words cannot with any probability be applied to David. Of the parted garments Adam Clarke observes that the soldiers knew nothing of this scripture and yet fulfilled it to the letter, dividing the outer garment in four and casting lots for the seamless tunic; Charles Ellicott answers that the two words of the verse are synonyms for one and the same article of dress, so that the gospel application adds a refinement not present in the psalm.
19:
The renewed petition draws from Adam Clarke the fullest doctrinal statement in the psalm, and it stands oddly beside his refusals a few verses earlier. Following an old father he says it is the humanity of our Lord which here speaks to his divinity, and lays down the rule that every expression of weakness in the psalm belongs to the human nature: the man could not have worked those miracles, and the God in that man could not have suffered those sufferings, yet one person appears to do and to suffer all. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the words, taking the sword for the deadly weapon of the enemy used by way of example, and observing that the hand of the dog is by the sense a paw. John Gill reads the lion either of the adversary overcome in the garden and on the cross or of the most powerful among the human enemies.

What is meant by the thing called his darling is answered three ways. Adam Clarke renders it my only one and takes it of the sufferer himself as the only human being ever produced without the agency of man, setting the first man formed from the dust against the second produced in the womb of the virgin. John Wesley takes it of his soul, so called because it was left alone and destitute of friends and helpers. Charles Ellicott keeps to usage: the word is used of an only child and also of a person left desolate, and stands here as a synonym for soul or life, as the Homeric poems say dear heart.

The last of the beasts sets Adam Clarke off on natural history. The name probably means the rhinoceros, he says, since no land animal but that one has a single horn; but there is a marine animal, the narwhal, a species of whale, whose fine curled ivory horn can be driven through the side of a ship, and one in his own museum measures seven feet four inches and is very beautiful. He adds from his old Psalter that the unicorn is one of the proudest beasts there is, so that it will die of indignation if it be held against its will. Charles Ellicott puts the creature at a buffalo or an antelope and then weighs three ways of construing what follows — that God hear him calling from among the horns, or that the prayer breaks off into exultant faith with thou hast heard me, or, with the old versions, that he be saved poor and humble as he is — preferring the first because it best preserves the parallelism. John Wesley says only that he was answered and delivered.
22:
All of them mark the turn and describe it in the same terms. Matthew Henry observes that the same speaker who began the psalm complaining ends it triumphing, and that as the first words of the complaint were used on the cross so the first words of the triumph are expressly applied to the same person in the epistle. C.H. Spurgeon puts it as weather: from a horrible tempest all is changed into calm, the darkness of Calvary passing away at length from the face of nature and from the soul of the Redeemer; and he proposes that the whole passage still be regarded as part of a soliloquy uttered in the mind during the last few moments before the death. Keil and Delitzsch say of the verses that follow simply that this stanza is the evangel itself. On the brethren John Gill excludes the kinsmen according to the flesh and settles on the apostles, whom he called brethren after the resurrection; John Wesley notes that the title does not fit David, who never gives it to any but near kindred, as it fits one who extends it to all his disciples.

Who is being summoned to praise is disputed at once. John Gill reports that some Jewish interpreters take those who fear the Lord as the proselytes among the Gentiles, distinguished from the seed of Jacob named beside them, and rejects it: the phrase covers all the people of God, whether Jews or Gentiles. Adam Clarke takes the other side, reading the whole as an exhortation to the Jews to profit by the preaching of the gospel, and thinking that the fearers may indeed be the Gentiles and particularly the proselytes, since the seed of Jacob and the seed of Israel are then named separately. Keil and Delitzsch address it to the whole of Israel so far as it fears the God of revelation. On the ground given for the praise they are more exact than the rest: the word rendered affliction means a bowing down and is the proper term for the Passion, so that the ancient versions which render it cry are in error; and the word for abhorrence shows that the sufferer had felt the wrath of God, which has now changed into a love that sends help. Adam Clarke hears in it an answer to the bystanders, that though they despised him in his humiliation God has received him in the character of a sufferer for sin.

The vows and the meal divide the spiritual readers from the literal. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to spiritualise: it is not necessary to suppose that the paying of vows here is purely ethical rather than a ritual act, for being rescued he will bring the thank-offerings which he vowed to God in the extremest peril. Charles Ellicott is equally concrete, preferring the afflicted to the meek and holding that the word, standing among so many expressions for worship, points to the Levites, while the figure of the banquet is suggested by the feast that followed a great sacrifice. Adam Clarke keeps the sacrificial logic but turns it forward, since those who offered the sacrifice fed on what they offered. John Gill and John Wesley read the eating and the satisfying wholly of spiritual blessings. Adam Clarke also distinguishes the two congregations, the smaller assembly of the earlier verse from the great assembly here, and assigns the first to the Jews and the second to the Gentiles; John Wesley answers that the great congregation is the universal church of both. Keil and Delitzsch close by observing how far the results described here transcend the historical reality of David’s experience, since the heathen who had grown forgetful are to recollect themselves again.
27:
The turning of the nations is read by all of them as prophecy, and by one as the key to the psalm. John Wesley calls it an evident prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles and a clear proof that the psalm speaks immediately of Christ, to whom alone this and various other passages belong; and at the close he says the last verse gives the key to the whole, teaching that the writer speaks not of himself but of things to be done in after ages. John Gill confines the promise to the elect among the Gentiles in the farthest parts of the world. Adam Clarke presses it further than either: not only shall the nations receive the gospel as a revelation from God, but each family shall embrace it for their own salvation. John Wesley unfolds the remembering into a list — their former wickedness, and particularly their worship of dead and impotent idols; their forgotten obligations; and the gracious words and glorious works of Christ, of which, he adds, several of them may have been eye and ear witnesses. Keil and Delitzsch account for the same remembering by saying that a knowledge of God exists among the heathen which the announcement of this rescue will bring back into their consciousness.

The hardest verse of the close is emended by two of them in opposite directions. Adam Clarke observes that where our text says none can keep alive his own soul, the Latin, Syriac, Greek, Ethiopic, Arabic and old English versions all read instead that my soul shall live to him and my seed shall serve him, and that his old Psalter follows them closely; he believes this the true reading, notes the three small changes of letter it requires, and takes the words as the psalmist’s own vow that he will live to this Saviour while he lives and that his spiritual posterity will serve him through all generations. Charles Ellicott changes the same verse on quite different grounds. The mention of the fat ones of the earth among those who eat seems to him certainly out of place and injurious to the parallelism, so that the text must be altered either to make earth’s mourners the eaters or to bow the fat ones before him in a separate clause; and the closing words he renders not of those already dead but of the man who cannot keep his own soul alive, that is, of one too poor to keep body and soul together.

Who the fat upon earth are is disputed among the rest. John Gill takes them for the rich, and for princes and rulers, while reporting a Jewish reading that inverts the clause so that the meek eat all the fat of the earth; he adds that the word carries the sense of ashes, since some lands are fattened by ashes strewn on them, and observes that the rich and great are themselves but dust and ashes. Adam Clarke expects the great and even kings to embrace the gospel and count it their highest honour. John Wesley has them feeding on the bread of life, and takes those who go down to the dust for all mankind, since none escapes death. Keil and Delitzsch return to the eating and call it a meal that satisfies the soul, brought about by the mighty act of rescue. Of the seed that serves, Charles Ellicott renders that posterity shall serve him and that the story shall be told to the coming generation, preferring this to a reference some find to a census because the parallelism is against it; John Gill notes the old versions which read my seed and the paraphrase which makes it the seed of Abraham, and answers that the seed intended is chiefly Gentile; and Adam Clarke says only that they shall be called after the name of Christ.
